authoredSolutions.31: Warming a sulphide salt with dilute \(H_{2}SO_{4}\) liberates \(H_{2}S\), which blackens lead acetate paper, so Statement-I is a correct description of the confirmatory test for \(S^{2-}\). The black solid is lead sulphide, \(Pb(CH_{3}COO)_{2}+H_{2}S \rightarrow PbS \downarrow + 2CH_{3}COOH\), not lead sulphite; lead sulphite \(PbSO_{3}\) is white. Statement-II therefore gives the wrong product, so Statement-I is true but Statement-II is false, which is option (C).
authoredSolutions.32: The figure shows benzoyl chloride being converted to benzaldehyde using \(H_{2}\) over palladium supported on barium sulphate. Catalytic hydrogenation of an acyl chloride to an aldehyde over poisoned (partially deactivated) \(Pd/BaSO_{4}\) is the Rosenmund reduction; the poison stops the reaction at the aldehyde stage instead of going on to the alcohol. Wolff-Kishner reduces \(C=O\) to \(CH_{2}\), Stephen reduction converts a nitrile to an aldehyde, and Etard oxidises a methyl arene, so the answer is option (A).
authoredSolutions.33: Fehling's reagent gives a reddish-brown precipitate of \(Cu_{2}O\) only with reducing sugars, i.e. sugars that retain a free aldehydic or ketonic (hemiacetal) centre. Glucose, maltose and lactose all have a free anomeric hemiacetal carbon and are reducing. In sucrose the anomeric carbons of both glucose and fructose are locked in the glycosidic linkage, so it is non-reducing and gives no precipitate, which is option (A).
authoredSolutions.34: Both statements are individually correct: covalent and ionic radii do increase down group 15, and there is a large jump from \(N\) to \(P\) whereas from \(As\) to \(Bi\) the increase is small. However the Reason only states the general downward trend; it does not account for the anomaly, which arises from the poor shielding by the completely filled \(d\) and \(f\) orbitals present in the heavier members. Hence both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A), which is option (B).
authoredSolutions.35: Option (A) is the cyclopropenyl cation: a planar cyclic system with 2 delocalised \(\pi\) electrons, satisfying Huckel's \(4n+2\) rule with \(n=0\), so it is aromatic. Option (B) is the cyclopentadienyl cation (4 \(\pi\) electrons) and option (C) is the cyclopropenyl anion (4 \(\pi\) electrons); both are antiaromatic and strongly destabilised. Option (D), cyclohexa-1,3-diene, is merely non-aromatic. On the aromatic > non-aromatic > antiaromatic stability scale the aromatic cyclopropenyl cation is the most stable, so the answer is option (A).
authoredSolutions.36: A lanthanoid ion is diamagnetic only when its \(4f\) subshell has no unpaired electrons. \(La^{3+}\) is \(4f^{0}\) and \(Ce^{4+}\) is also \(4f^{0}\), so both have all electrons paired and are diamagnetic. \(Nd^{3+}\) is \(4f^{3}\) and \(Eu^{3+}\) is \(4f^{6}\), both with unpaired electrons, so every option containing them is ruled out; the correct pair is option (B).
authoredSolutions.37: In acidified aqueous solution \(AlCl_{3}\) does not stay as the covalent dimer; the small, highly charged \(Al^{3+}\) ion is strongly hydrated and exists as the hexaaqua ion \(\left[Al(H_{2}O)_{6}\right]^{3+}\). With a coordination number of six the ion adopts an octahedral geometry, so the answer is option (A).
authoredSolutions.38: Orbitals of equal energy are by definition degenerate, so Statement-I is true. In a one-electron species such as the hydrogen atom there is no inter-electronic repulsion, so the energy depends only on the principal quantum number \(n\); therefore \(3s\), \(3p\) and \(3d\) all have the same energy and ARE degenerate. Statement-II claims the opposite and is false, so Statement-I is true but Statement-II is false, which is option (A).
authoredSolutions.39: A vinylic halide has the halogen bonded directly to an \(sp^{2}\) carbon that is part of a carbon-carbon double bond. Option (A) is cyclohexylidene-methyl halide, \(C_{6}H_{10}=CH-X\), where \(X\) sits on the doubly bonded \(sp^{2}\) carbon, so it is vinylic. Option (B) has \(CH_{2}X\) on the ring double bond and option (D) has \(X\) on the \(sp^{3}\) carbon next to the double bond, so both are allylic, while option (C) is an aryl halide; the answer is option (A).
authoredSolutions.40: In 4-methylpent-2-enal the \(-CHO\) carbon is C-1, the double bond runs from C-2 to C-3, and a methyl branch sits on C-4 of a five-carbon parent chain, giving \(CH_{3}-CH(CH_{3})-CH=CH-CHO\). Option (D) is exactly this structure. Option (A) is 3-methylpent-4-enal, option (B) is 3-methylpent-2-enal and option (C) is 2-methylpent-2-enal, so the answer is option (D).
authoredSolutions.41: Count the steric number for each species. \(BrF_{5}\) has 5 bond pairs and 1 lone pair (\(AB_{5}E\)), giving a square pyramidal shape (IV); \(H_{2}O\) is \(AB_{2}E_{2}\) and is bent (III); \(ClF_{3}\) is \(AB_{3}E_{2}\) and is T-shaped (I); \(SF_{4}\) is \(AB_{4}E\) and is see-saw (II). The matching (A)-IV, (B)-III, (C)-I, (D)-II corresponds to option (D).
authoredSolutions.42: Bromobenzene with \(Mg\)/ether gives phenylmagnesium bromide, which on treatment with \(CO_{2}\) followed by \(H^{+}\) gives benzoic acid. Heating benzoic acid with ammonia gives benzamide. Benzamide with \(Br_{2}\) and \(NaOH\) undergoes the Hofmann bromamide degradation, losing one carbon to give the primary amine with one fewer carbon, namely aniline. The final product A is aniline, which is option (B).
authoredSolutions.43: Both routes convert toluene to benzaldehyde without over-oxidation to benzoic acid. In the upper route the reagent is used with acetic anhydride at 273-283 K: \(CrO_{3}\) gives benzylidene diacetate, which on acid hydrolysis yields benzaldehyde, so \(A = CrO_{3}\). The lower route runs in \(CS_{2}\), which is the Etard reaction using chromyl chloride to form a chromium complex that hydrolyses to benzaldehyde, so \(B = CrO_{2}Cl_{2}\). The answer is option (B).
authoredSolutions.44: \(CH_{2}=CH-CH_{2}-Cl\) (allyl chloride) has the halogen on the carbon adjacent to the double bond, so the Assertion is true. The Reason misstates the definition: in an allylic halide the halogen is attached to an \(sp^{3}\) carbon next to a \(C=C\); a halogen on an \(sp^{2}\) doubly bonded carbon defines a vinylic halide instead. Hence (A) is true but (R) is false, which is option (A).
authoredSolutions.45: Naphthalene is a non-volatile solute in benzene, so it lowers the vapour pressure of the solution below that of pure benzene. Depression of freezing point is a colligative property given by \(\Delta T_{f}=K_{f}\,m\), which is positive for any non-volatile solute. The freezing point of benzene therefore decreases, which is option (D).
authoredSolutions.46: Write the neutral configuration and remove electrons from \(4s\) first. \(Cr\) is \([Ar]3d^{5}4s^{1}\), so \(Cr^{2+}\) is \(3d^{4}\) (III). \(Mn\) is \([Ar]3d^{5}4s^{2}\), so \(Mn^{+}\) is \(3d^{5}4s^{1}\) (IV). \(Ni\) is \([Ar]3d^{8}4s^{2}\), so \(Ni^{2+}\) is \(3d^{8}\) (I). \(V\) is \([Ar]3d^{3}4s^{2}\), so \(V^{+}\) is \(3d^{3}4s^{1}\) (II). The matching (A)-III, (B)-IV, (C)-I, (D)-II is option (B).
authoredSolutions.47: Propyne has an acidic terminal \(\equiv C-H\), so sodium metal deprotonates it to give sodium propynide, \(CH_{3}-C \equiv C^{-}Na^{+}\); this is A. The final product C is \(CH_{3}-C \equiv C-CH_{2}CH_{2}CH_{3}\) and \(NaBr\) is co-produced, so B must be a primary alkyl bromide supplying the three-carbon \(n\)-propyl group. The acetylide displaces bromide from \(CH_{3}CH_{2}CH_{2}Br\) in an \(S_{N}2\) alkylation, so the answer is option (A).
authoredSolutions.48: Reagent A must convert aniline into benzenediazonium chloride, which requires nitrous acid generated in situ, i.e. \(NaNO_{2}+HCl\) at \(0-5^{\circ}C\); this rules out option (A). Reagent B is the coupling component used in alkaline medium in the dye test that confirms an aromatic primary amine. Coupling of benzenediazonium chloride with 2-naphthol (\(\beta\)-naphthol) in \(NaOH\) gives 1-(phenylazo)-2-naphthol, the brilliant scarlet-red azo dye; phenol gives an orange dye and aniline a yellow one. The answer is option (D).
authoredSolutions.49: If nitrogen and sulphur are also present, the Lassaigne's extract contains \(NaCN\) and \(Na_{2}S\). Adding \(AgNO_{3}\) directly would precipitate white \(AgCN\) and black \(Ag_{2}S\) alongside the silver halide and vitiate the test. Boiling with dilute \(HNO_{3}\) first decomposes \(NaCN\) to \(HCN\) and \(Na_{2}S\) to \(H_{2}S\), both of which escape as gases, leaving only the halide to react with \(AgNO_{3}\). The answer is option (D).
authoredSolutions.50: (A) is correct: ethane-1,2-diamine (en) is bidentate and forms a five-membered chelate ring. (B) is correct: aluminium is obtained by Hall-Heroult electrolysis of \(Al_{2}O_{3}\) dissolved in molten cryolite. (C) is correct: silver is leached from its ore as the complex \(\left[Ag(CN)_{2}\right]^{-}\). (D) is wrong as written because Wilkinson's catalyst is \(\left[RhCl(PPh_{3})_{3}\right]\), containing triphenylphosphine rather than phosphine \(PH_{3}\), and (E) is wrong because the EDTA stability constants of \(Ca^{2+}\) and \(Mg^{2+}\) differ appreciably. Only (A), (B) and (C) are correct, which is option (C).
authoredSolutions.51: For a first order reaction the rate is directly proportional to concentration, so \(\frac{[A]_{10}}{[A]_{20}}=\frac{0.04}{0.03}=\frac{4}{3}\) over the 10 minute interval. Hence \(k=\frac{2.303}{10}\log\frac{4}{3}=\frac{2.303}{10}(2 \times 0.3010-0.4771)=\frac{2.303 \times 0.1249}{10}=0.02876\ \text{min}^{-1}\). Then \(t_{1/2}=\frac{0.693}{k}=\frac{0.693}{0.02876}=24.1\), so the half-life is about 24 minutes.
authoredSolutions.52: Precipitation begins when the ionic product just equals \(K_{sp}\): \(\left[Mg^{2+}\right]\left[OH^{-}\right]^{2}=1 \times 10^{-11}\). With \(\left[Mg^{2+}\right]=0.10\ M\), \(\left[OH^{-}\right]^{2}=\frac{1 \times 10^{-11}}{0.10}=1 \times 10^{-10}\), so \(\left[OH^{-}\right]=1 \times 10^{-5}\ M\). Therefore \(pOH=5\) and \(pH=14-5=9\).
authoredSolutions.53: Read the graph with \(V\) on the vertical axis: \(A(10\ kPa,10\ dm^{3})\), \(B(10\ kPa,30\ dm^{3})\), \(C(30\ kPa,10\ dm^{3})\). Along \(A \rightarrow B\) the pressure is constant, so the gas expands doing \(P\Delta V=10 \times 20=200\ J\) of work. Along \(B \rightarrow C\) the straight line is \(P=40-V\), and \(\int_{30}^{10}(40-V)\,dV=-400\ J\), while \(C \rightarrow A\) is isochoric with zero work. The net work done by the gas is \(200-400=-200\ J\), i.e. the magnitude of the enclosed triangle \(\tfrac{1}{2} \times 20 \times 20=200\), so the total work done on the gas in the cycle is \(200\ J\).
authoredSolutions.54: IUPAC systematic names use the numerical roots un = 1, bi = 2, tri = 3 and so on, with the suffix -ium. 'Unununnium' reads un-un-un-ium, giving atomic number 111 (now named roentgenium). Element 111 lies just below gold in the periodic table and therefore belongs to group 11, so \(n=11\).
authoredSolutions.55: Molecular orbital theory conserves orbital count: combining \(N\) atomic orbitals always produces exactly \(N\) molecular orbitals. Each atom of the diatomic contributes one \(2s\) and three \(2p\) orbitals, i.e. 4 atomic orbitals, so the two atoms together supply 8 atomic orbitals. These combine to give 8 molecular orbitals (4 bonding and 4 antibonding).
authoredSolutions.57: Semicarbazide is \(H_{2}N-NH-CO-NH_{2}\) and contains three nitrogen atoms. Only the terminal \(-NH_{2}\) of the hydrazine end is nucleophilic enough to condense with a carbonyl, so ethanal gives the semicarbazone \(CH_{3}-CH=N-NH-CO-NH_{2}\) with loss of water. No nitrogen is lost in the condensation, so the product contains 3 nitrogen atoms.
authoredSolutions.58: Convert the area to \(cm^{2}\): \(0.05\ m^{2}=0.05 \times 10^{4}=500\ cm^{2}\). The volume of the coating is \(500 \times 0.05=25\ cm^{3}\), so its mass is \(25 \times 7.9=197.5\ g\). Moles of silver \(=197.5/108=1.829\), and the number of atoms is \(1.829 \times 6.022 \times 10^{23}=11.01 \times 10^{23}\). Hence the answer is 11.
authoredSolutions.59: Manganese goes from \(+7\) in \(MnO_{4}^{-}\) to \(+4\) in \(MnO_{2}\), gaining 3 electrons each, so 2 permanganate ions accept 6 electrons. Iodide loses one electron each, so \(b=6\) and \(x=3\), with \(y=2\). Balancing charge gives left \(=2(-1)+6(-1)=-8\), so the right must also be \(-8\) and \(z=8\); checking hydrogen fixes \(c=4\), and oxygen balances as \(8+4=4+8\). Therefore \(z=8\).
authoredSolutions.60: Moles required \(=M \times V=0.35\ mol\ L^{-1} \times 0.250\ L=0.0875\ mol\). Mass \(=\) moles \(\times\) molar mass \(=0.0875 \times 82.02=7.17675\ g\). Rounded to two decimal places the required mass of sodium acetate is \(7.18\ g\).
authoredSolutions.121: Differential extraction separates a compound from an aqueous solution by shaking with an immiscible organic solvent in which the compound is far more soluble, so it is governed purely by the relative solubility in two different solvents. Sublimation exploits the ability to pass directly from solid to vapour, distillation exploits differences in boiling point, and column chromatography exploits differential adsorption on a stationary phase. Hence the answer is option (D).
authoredSolutions.122: Phenol treated with chloroform and aqueous sodium hydroxide at 340 K undergoes the Reimer-Tiemann reaction. Hydroxide deprotonates \(CHCl_{3}\) to give dichlorocarbene \(:CCl_{2}\), which attacks the electron-rich ortho position of the phenoxide ion; hydrolysis of the resulting benzal chloride gives the \(-CHO\) group, producing salicylaldehyde. The reagent pair is therefore \(HCCl_{3}\) and \(NaOH\), option (D); \(CO_{2}/NaOH\) would instead give salicylic acid by the Kolbe reaction.
authoredSolutions.123: A high concentration of a strong nucleophile favours the bimolecular pathway, and a secondary alkyl halide without bulky substituents is sterically accessible for backside attack, so Statement-I correctly describes \(S_{N}2\) behaviour. Ethanol in large excess is a weak nucleophile but a polar protic solvent that stabilises the carbocation and the leaving halide by solvation, so solvolysis of a secondary halide proceeds by the unimolecular \(S_{N}1\) route, making Statement-II true as well. Both statements are true, which is option (D).
authoredSolutions.124: m-Chlorobenzaldehyde has no \(\alpha\)-hydrogen, so with concentrated (50%) \(KOH\) it undergoes the Cannizzaro reaction, a self oxidation-reduction of two aldehyde molecules. One molecule is oxidised to the carboxylate, m-chlorobenzoate, and the other is reduced to the primary alcohol, m-chlorobenzyl alcohol. The chlorine substituent is not displaced under these conditions, so the products are shown in option (B).
authoredSolutions.125: Acidic strength of group 16 hydrides increases down the group, \(H_{2}O<H_{2}S<H_{2}Se<H_{2}Te\), so the Assertion that \(H_{2}Te\) is more acidic than \(H_{2}S\) is true. Going down the group the central atom gets larger, the \(E-H\) overlap gets poorer and the bond dissociation enthalpy falls, so the Reason is also true. Weaker \(H-Te\) bonding is precisely why the proton is released more readily, so the Reason correctly explains the Assertion, which is option (B).
authoredSolutions.126: Acid-catalysed hydration of 1-methylcyclohexene follows Markovnikov's rule through the more stable tertiary carbocation, so \(OH\) adds to the substituted carbon giving 1-methylcyclohexan-1-ol as product A. Hydroboration with \(B_{2}H_{6}\) followed by oxidation with alkaline \(H_{2}O_{2}\) is anti-Markovnikov and syn, placing \(OH\) on the less substituted carbon to give trans-2-methylcyclohexan-1-ol as product B. This pairing appears in option (B).
authoredSolutions.127: The structure is \(CH_{3}-CH(NH_{2})-CH_{2}-CN\). The nitrile group is the principal characteristic group and its carbon is always C-1, so numbering runs \(C \equiv N\) (C-1), \(CH_{2}\) (C-2), \(CH(NH_{2})\) (C-3), \(CH_{3}\) (C-4). The parent chain of four carbons ending in \(-CN\) is butanenitrile with an amino substituent at C-3, giving 3-aminobutanenitrile, option (C).
authoredSolutions.128: Benzene with concentrated \(HNO_{3}/H_{2}SO_{4}\) at 323-333 K gives nitrobenzene, and \(Sn/HCl\) reduces the nitro group to give aniline, so A is aniline. Aniline with \(NaNO_{2}/HCl\) at 273-278 K gives benzenediazonium chloride, which is a weak electrophile and couples only with strongly activated rings. With phenol it attacks the para position to give p-hydroxyazobenzene, an orange azo dye, so B is \(HO-C_{6}H_{4}-N=N-C_{6}H_{5}\), which is option (C).
authoredSolutions.129: A square pyramidal shape arises from an \(AB_{5}E\) system: six electron domains in an octahedral arrangement with one of them a lone pair. \(BrF_{5}\) has bromine with 5 bond pairs and 1 lone pair, so it is square pyramidal. \(PCl_{5}\) and \(PF_{5}\) are \(AB_{5}\) with no lone pair and are trigonal bipyramidal, while \(\left[Ni(CN)_{4}\right]^{2-}\) is square planar, so the answer is option (C).
authoredSolutions.130: In \(K_{2}Cr_{2}O_{7}\) chromium is in the \(+6\) state and in \(KMnO_{4}\) manganese is in the \(+7\) state, so both metal centres have a \(d^{0}\) configuration. With no \(d\) electrons present, \(d \rightarrow d\) transitions are impossible in either compound. Their intense colours instead come from ligand-to-metal charge transfer, in which an electron is momentarily transferred from an oxide ion to the metal, so the answer is option (A).
authoredSolutions.131: Alkaline oxidative fusion of \(MnO_{2}\) with \(KOH\) and an oxidant such as \(KNO_{3}\) or air gives the dark green manganate ion, \(2MnO_{2}+4KOH+O_{2} \rightarrow 2K_{2}MnO_{4}+2H_{2}O\), so A is \(MnO_{4}^{2-}\). Electrolytic oxidation of the manganate in alkaline solution removes one more electron to give the purple permanganate ion, \(MnO_{4}^{2-} \rightarrow MnO_{4}^{-}+e^{-}\), so B is \(MnO_{4}^{-}\). The answer is option (B).
authoredSolutions.132: Mole fraction of a component is its number of moles divided by the total number of moles of all components in the solution. Here the solution contains A, B and C, so the total is \(n_{A}+n_{B}+n_{C}\). Therefore \(x_{C}=\frac{n_{C}}{n_{A}+n_{B}+n_{C}}\), which is option (B).
authoredSolutions.133: Chemical reactivity across a period is not monotonic: it is high on the extreme left where metals readily lose electrons, falls to a minimum in the middle of the period, rises again among the halogens which readily gain electrons, and drops to almost nil for the noble gases of group 18. Statement-I is therefore false. Statement-II is true, since group 1 elements form strongly basic oxides such as \(Na_{2}O\) while group 17 elements form acidic oxides such as \(Cl_{2}O_{7}\). Statement-I false and Statement-II true is option (C).
authoredSolutions.134: Decacarbonyldimanganese(0) is \(Mn_{2}(CO)_{10}\), a dimer in which the ten carbonyls are shared equally, five on each manganese, and the two metal atoms are joined by an unsupported \(Mn-Mn\) bond. Each manganese is therefore bonded to five \(CO\) ligands plus one manganese, a coordination number of six. Six equivalent donors around the metal give an octahedral geometry, which is option (A).
authoredSolutions.135: Experimentally \(NH_{3}\) has \(\mu=1.46\ D\) while \(NF_{3}\) has only \(0.24\ D\), so Statement-I is false despite fluorine being the more electronegative element. The reason is that in \(NH_{3}\) the lone pair orbital dipole points the SAME way as the resultant of the three \(N-H\) bond dipoles and reinforces it, whereas in \(NF_{3}\) the \(N-F\) bond dipoles point away from nitrogen and OPPOSE the lone pair dipole, largely cancelling it. Statement-II reverses these two directions and is therefore also false, giving option (B).
authoredSolutions.136: A carbocation is electron deficient, so it is stabilised by alkyl groups through the \(+I\) inductive effect and, more importantly, by hyperconjugation with the \(C-H\) bonds on the adjacent carbons. The tertiary butyl cation has nine \(\alpha\) hydrogens available for hyperconjugation, the isopropyl cation six, the ethyl cation three and the methyl cation none. Stability therefore falls in the order \(3^{\circ}>2^{\circ}>1^{\circ}>\) methyl, which is option (C).
authoredSolutions.137: Depression of freezing point is \(\Delta T_{f}=i\,K_{f}\,m\), so compare \(i \times\) moles \(\times K_{f}\) for an equal mass of solvent. Acetic acid (\(M=60\)) gives 3 mol and benzoic acid (\(M=122\)) gives 1.48 mol, while glucose gives 1 mol; \(K_{f}\) is 5.12 for benzene against only 1.86 for water. In benzene both acids dimerise through hydrogen bonding so \(i \approx 0.5\), whereas in water acetic acid is only very slightly ionised so \(i \approx 1\). This gives roughly \(0.5 \times 3 \times 5.12=7.7\) for (B) against \(3 \times 1.86=5.6\) for (A), \(0.5 \times 1.48 \times 5.12=3.8\) for (C) and \(1.86\) for (D), so option (B) shows the largest depression.
authoredSolutions.138: Chromyl chloride is hydrolysed by alkali to the chromate ion: \(CrO_{2}Cl_{2}+4NaOH \rightarrow Na_{2}CrO_{4}+2NaCl+2H_{2}O\), which balances for Cr, Na, Cl, O and H, so \(A=Na_{2}CrO_{4}\). Acidified chromate treated with hydrogen peroxide gives the deep blue peroxide \(CrO_{5}\) (chromium peroxide, containing two peroxo linkages): \(Na_{2}CrO_{4}+2HCl+2H_{2}O_{2} \rightarrow CrO_{5}+2NaCl+3H_{2}O\), where oxygen balances as \(4+4=5+3\). Hence \(B=CrO_{5}\) and the answer is option (A).
authoredSolutions.139: Down group 15 the \(E-H\) bond dissociation enthalpy falls as the central atom grows, so thermal stability decreases in the order \(NH_{3}>PH_{3}>AsH_{3}>SbH_{3}>BiH_{3}\), making (A) correct. Weaker \(E-H\) bonds also make the hydride a better hydrogen donor, so reducing power increases in the order \(NH_{3}<PH_{3}<AsH_{3}<SbH_{3}<BiH_{3}\), making (B) correct. Statement (C) reverses this, since \(BiH_{3}\) is the strongest reductant and \(NH_{3}\) the weakest, and (D) is wrong because basicity DECREASES down the group as the lone pair becomes more diffuse. Only (A) and (B) are correct, option (C).
authoredSolutions.140: The more positive the standard reduction potential, the greater the tendency of the species to be reduced and hence the stronger its oxidising power. The given values are \(ClO_{4}^{-}\) 1.19 V, \(IO_{4}^{-}\) 1.65 V and \(BrO_{4}^{-}\) 1.74 V. Arranging in decreasing \(E^{\circ}\) gives \(BrO_{4}^{-}>IO_{4}^{-}>ClO_{4}^{-}\), which is option (B); perbromate is anomalously the strongest because of the poor shielding by the filled \(3d\) subshell in bromine.
authoredSolutions.141: An octahedral complex is optically active only when it has neither a plane nor a centre of symmetry. \(\left[Co(en)_{3}\right]^{3+}\) is the classic tris-chelate propeller and is chiral. For the \(M(AA)_{2}X_{2}\) type, the cis isomer is chiral while the trans isomer has a plane of symmetry, so cis-\(\left[Cr(ox)_{2}Cl_{2}\right]^{3-}\), cis-\(\left[Pt(en)_{2}Cl_{2}\right]^{2+}\) and cis-\(\left[Co(en)_{2}Cl_{2}\right]^{+}\) are all optically active while both trans complexes are not. That gives 4 optically active complexes.
authoredSolutions.142: The concentration of \(N_{2}O_{5}\) falls by \(3-2.75=0.25\ mol\ L^{-1}\) in 30 minutes, so \(-\frac{d\left[N_{2}O_{5}\right]}{dt}=\frac{0.25}{30}=8.33 \times 10^{-3}\ mol\ L^{-1}\ min^{-1}\). From the stoichiometry \(2N_{2}O_{5} \rightarrow 4NO_{2}+O_{2}\), the rate of reaction is \(\frac{1}{2}\) of this and \(\frac{d\left[NO_{2}\right]}{dt}=4 \times \frac{1}{2} \times 8.33 \times 10^{-3}\), i.e. twice the rate of disappearance of \(N_{2}O_{5}\). This gives \(16.67 \times 10^{-3}\ mol\ L^{-1}\ min^{-1}\), so \(x=16.67\).
authoredSolutions.143: Apply Hess's law by combining the given equations so that they add up to the target. Multiply the carbon equation by 3 to get \(3C+\frac{3}{2}O_{2} \rightarrow 3CO\) with \(\Delta H=3(-110)=-330\ kJ\), and reverse the iron equation to get \(Fe_{2}O_{3} \rightarrow 2Fe+\frac{3}{2}O_{2}\) with \(\Delta H=+822\ kJ\). Adding them cancels the oxygen and reproduces \(3C+Fe_{2}O_{3} \rightarrow 2Fe+3CO\), so \(\Delta H^{\circ}=-330+822=+492\ kJ/mol\).

authoredSolutions.164: For differentiability on \(R\), \(f\) must be continuous and have matching derivatives at \(x=1\). Continuity: \(1+3+a = b+2 \Rightarrow b = a+2\).
